summary: Defines an interoperability profile for the user equipment, such as videophones and apps, used with Video Relay Service. In that service a sign language user talks over video with an interpreter, who then speaks with the hearing person by telephone. The profile aims to let different vendors' equipment and relay providers work together. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Some deaf people use video calls to talk with an interpreter who then phones the other person. This document is the rulebook so any brand of video phone can connect to any relay service.

subtitle: The rulebook that lets any sign-language videophone work with any video relay provider.

tldr.problem: In Video Relay Service, a sign language user talks over video to an interpreter who phones the hearing person. Without a standard, a videophone works only with some providers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles SIP and WebRTC-style media for the Relay User Equipment (RUE), and adds two small HTTPS and JSON web services for choosing a provider and fetching its configuration.
tldr.outcome: A conforming device can register, place and receive relay and direct video calls, use real-time text, reach emergency services and sync contacts with any conforming provider.

facts.label: Real-time text interval
facts.value: 300 ms, one original plus two redundant generations

facts.label: Minimum call timeout
facts.value: Not less than the 3 minute SIP INVITE default

today: RFC 9248 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022. It does not obsolete or update any other RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What the RUE Profile Covers
sections.content:
Video Relay Service (VRS) lets people with hearing or speech disabilities who use sign language, such as American Sign Language, talk with voice telephone users through video equipment. A Communications Assistant (CA), a sign-language interpreter working for a provider, signs with the user over video and speaks with the hearing person over an ordinary telephone call.

RFC 9248 is a profile of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and related media protocols for the Relay User Equipment (RUE): the videophone, app or other device the signing user has. It lists the minimal set of call flows and IETF and ITU-T standards that must be supported, gives guidance where those standards leave options open, and defines minimal and extended capabilities.

Both interpreted calls and direct subscriber-to-subscriber calls are supported. The RFC only describes the interface between the device and the provider, not any other interface the provider has. Backwards compatibility with older equipment is accommodated in places but is not a requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: A deaf person uses a video phone to sign to an interpreter, and the interpreter phones the other person. This rulebook says how the video phone must behave so it works with any interpreter company.

sections.title: Baseline Requirements
sections.content:
Every HTTP connection in the profile MUST use HTTPS, and both HTTPS and all SIP connections MUST use TLS conforming to at least RFC 7525 and MUST support RFC 8446. Text payloads not otherwise constrained MUST be UTF-8. Implementations MUST support both IPv4 and IPv6, but dual-stack support is not required.

On the SIP side, a device must follow the core SIP standards, including base SIP, server location, offer/answer, outbound, privacy, UPDATE and early media, plus full ICE (an implementation MAY interwork with ICE-lite peers), REFER and the Replaces header. It MUST put a User-Agent header identifying the application, platform and version in every request, and a matching Server header in responses. Mobile implementations MUST support RFC 8599 as at least one way to wake the client from the background.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook starts with safety and basics: every connection is locked with encryption, text is written the same way everywhere, and devices say what program they are.

sections.title: Registration and Calls
sections.content:
When a device starts, it first runs the configuration step (see below), then registers with a SIP registrar at its provider, following RFC 3261 and the SIP Outbound mechanism of RFC 5626. The registration URI is built from the configured user name, or from the phone number, plus the provider domain. The DNS entry for the provider MUST contain NAPTR records, and one MUST name TLS as the preferred SIP transport. The registrar MAY use SIP digest authentication, and RFC 8760 with SHA-512 digests MUST be supported. If credentials are rejected, the device fetches a fresh configuration, and if those also fail it stops trying and tells the user.

Outgoing calls follow the normal SIP call flows and go through the configured outbound proxy. Anonymous calls MUST be supported. A caller must not give up on an unanswered call in less than the default 3 minute SIP INVITE timeout, so the call can reach a videomail server. Phone numbers are written as SIP URIs with ;user=phone and a global number without visual separators. Dial strings that are not E.164 numbers, such as 411, become dialstring URIs.

For incoming calls, the device MUST accept only calls sent by a proxy named in its configuration. If several devices register the same SIP URI, the provider MUST fork the call to all of them so they ring together; the first to answer with 200 OK gets the call and the others are cancelled.

Mid-call, devices MUST support re-INVITE to change media, and in-dialog REFER with the Replaces header for call transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: A video phone first signs in to its interpreter company, like logging in to a game. Then it can call out and receive calls, and if you have two phones with the same number, both ring and the first one picked up wins.

sections.title: Dial-Around, Owner Info and Emergency Calls
sections.content:
A user has a default provider but can pick another provider for any single call. This is called dial-around, and both providers and devices MUST support two kinds. In two-stage dial-around, the device calls the dial-around provider's "front-door" URI and then gives the number to call by signing or DTMF. In one-stage dial-around, the called number is placed in the To URI and Request-URI, but the domain is that of the dial-around provider.

To say who controls a device, the initial INVITE (or the 200 OK that accepts a call) carries a Call-Info header with purpose rue-owner, pointing to an xCard. The name, address, phone number and email address of the owner are expected to be supplied.

Emergency calls MUST follow RFC 6881. If the device cannot work out its own location, it MAY send the call without a Geolocation header and without a Route header. In that case, the provider MUST add the location and look up the route with a LoST server. Devices MUST also implement additional data per RFC 7852, including the data provider, device and owner/subscriber blocks. A device MAY send its location with REGISTER if the configuration says so, and the user MUST be offered an opt-out.
sections.plainLanguage: You can choose a different interpreter company for one call, like picking a different taxi company for one trip. For emergencies, the phone or the company must tell the helpers where you are.

sections.title: Media: Video, Text and Audio
sections.content:
The profile adopts the WebRTC media specifications but assumes an ordinary SIP call. A browser-based client can take part through a gateway that talks WebRTC to the browser and the RUE interface to the provider; the RFC does not specify that gateway.

  • Video: RFC 7742 applies with changes. Only H.264 is Mandatory to Implement, and VP8 is OPTIONAL, because older devices do not support VP8.
  • Real-time text: T.140 text via RFC 4103 MUST be supported, sent as one original and two redundant generations at a 300 ms transmission interval. RFC 9071 MUST also be supported, especially for emergency calls. For browser-based WebRTC peers, RFC 8865 is RECOMMENDED.
  • Audio: RFC 7874 applies.
  • DTMF: the audio/telephone-event type MUST be supported for event codes 0 through 11 (the digits 0 to 9 plus the star and pound keys).
  • Privacy: a local one-way mute for audio and video, with no signaling, MUST be provided, but the device MUST keep sending media packets such as silence or a blank screen so that NAT bindings stay alive.
  • Feedback: NACK, FIR and Picture Loss Indicator MUST be implemented. For older devices, SIP INFO messages with XML Picture Fast Update per RFC 5168 MUST be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture, the typed words and the sound each have a required format so every device understands them. You can mute yourself privately, but the phone keeps sending quiet blank pictures so the connection does not drop.

sections.title: Contacts and Video Mail
sections.content:
A device MUST be able to synchronize its contact list with one kept by the provider using CardDAV, although providers MAY choose not to offer CardDAV. The sync MUST be two-way, handling adds, changes and deletes at either end. Devices MUST also be able to export and import contacts as xCard XML through a web resource named by contacts-uri, using HTTPS GET or POST.

For video mail, the RFC specifies retrieval and a message-waiting indicator (MWI), but not message storage. Devices MUST support retrieval both by a SIP call to a given URI, using DTMF to manage the mailbox, and by a browser interface at an HTTPS URI. A provider that offers video mail MUST support at least one of the two, and MUST support MWI through message-summary subscriptions (RFC 3842). Messages containing video are reported with message-context-class multimedia-message.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone book can be kept in step with the company's copy, and if nobody answers, a caller can leave a video message that you fetch later. A little flag tells your phone a message is waiting.

sections.title: Provider List and Configuration Services
sections.content:
Provisioning is split into two web services, both described by normative OpenAPI 3.0 documents. If the text or examples disagree with the OpenAPI description, the OpenAPI description wins.

The provider list returns, for a country, a JSON list of providers, each with a display name and an entry point string. A new IANA registry maps two-letter country codes to the list's entry point. The RFC does not say who maintains the list. It suggests a regulator, an agreement among providers, or a user group. The device lets the user choose the country, and RUE implementations MUST include a user interaction step to choose a provider before registering with any of them.

The configuration service has two paths. ProviderConfig needs no credentials and returns signup, dial-around and help desk information. RueConfig uses the stored username and password and returns the settings the device needs. Both take a required instanceId that stays the same for each instance (a UUID is suggested) and an optional apiKey.

RueConfig items include phone-number and provider-domain (both required), plus optional lifetime (cache time in seconds), sip-password, user-name, display-name, outbound-proxies, mwi, videomail, contacts, carddav, sendLocationWithRegistration and ice-servers. Cached passwords MUST be cryptographically protected, and if no lifetime is given the device MUST fetch new data every time it starts.

Both services also report supported versions as major and minor numbers. Minor versions may only add things, and implementations MUST ignore members they do not implement.
sections.plainLanguage: First the phone asks for a list of interpreter companies in your country. Then it asks the one you pick for its settings, like a new phone getting its Wi-Fi and account details automatically.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The device must reach servers on public IP addresses and specific ports. Behind a default-deny firewall, the user has to arrange passage with the network manager, and the ports can differ between providers. The security considerations of all the other specifications this profile requires also apply.

A CA can hear and see the whole conversation even though it is nominally between two endpoints. The RFC says there is an expectation that the CA keeps it confidential, usually defined by contractual or legal requirements.

IANA created the "RUE Provider List" registry (Expert Review policy, with a regulator-operated list preferred) and added the rue-owner value to the Call-Info purpose parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The interpreter can see and hear everything in the call, so they are expected to keep it secret. Also, some strict office networks may block these calls unless the network manager lets them through.
